result: HHV-6A/6B are closely related viruses with approximately 90% sequence identity, possessing genomes with a unique region (U) of ~140 kb flanked by direct repeats (DR) of ~8 kb. The DRs contain telomeric repeat regions T1 and T2, with T2 facilitating integration into human telomeres through homology-dependent recombination.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature (Ablashi et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2014; Lindquester and Pellett, 1991; Zhang et al., 2017; Achour et al., 2009; Arbuckle et al., 2010; Wallaschek et al., 2016b). These claims describe established structural and functional features of HHV-6A/6B genomes that form the foundation for the study.

result: HHV-6A/6B infect over 90% of the global population in early childhood, and reactivation of acquired virus (acqHHV-6A/6B) causes serious conditions including viral encephalitis, DIHS/DRESS, aGVHD, and has been associated with multiple sclerosis and other chronic neurological conditions.
evaluation: Claims C6-C8 are supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Asano et al., 1994; Hall et al., 1994; Kondo et al., 1993; Ward and Gray, 1994; Zerr et al., 2005; Aihara et al., 2003; Eshki et al., 2009; Pritchett et al., 2012; Prusty, 2018; Yao et al., 2010; Yoshikawa et al., 2006). These claims establish the clinical significance of HHV-6A/6B infections and provide context for the study.

result: Approximately 1% of the population carries inherited chromosomally integrated HHV-6A/6B (iciHHV-6A/6B) with full-length viral genomes in every cell. iciHHV-6B is commonly found at 17p in European populations, while iciHHV-6A is commonly found at 22q in Japan.
evaluation: Claims C9-C11 are supported by multiple citations (Arbuckle et al., 2010; Daibata et al., 1999; Huang et al., 2014; Leong et al., 2007; Morris et al., 1999; Tanaka-Taya et al., 2004) and established knowledge about iciHHV-6A/6B prevalence and integration patterns. These claims provide essential background for understanding the study's focus on inherited viral genomes.

result: The presence of iciHHV-6A/6B causes localized telomere instability and has been associated with various health conditions including angina pectoris, unexplained infertility, increased risk of aGVHD following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, complications following solid organ transplantation with donor/recipient mismatch, and possibly increased risk of pre-eclampsia.
evaluation: Claims C12-C17 are supported by citations to prior literature (Huang et al., 2014; Wood and Royle, 2017; Zhang et al., 2016; Gravel et al., 2015; Miura et al., 2020; Hill et al., 2017; Weschke et al., 2020; Bonnafous et al., 2018; Bonnafous et al., 2020; Petit et al., 2020; Gaccioli et al., 2020). These claims establish the clinical relevance of iciHHV-6A/6B carrier status and motivate the study's investigation of viral genome dynamics.

result: iciHHV-6A/6B genomes can reactivate and be transmitted as acquired virus. Telomeres form t-loop structures stabilized by TRF2, which can be excised by the SLX1-4 endonuclease complex as t-circles, and unregulated excision results in critically short telomeres.
evaluation: Claims C18-C24 are supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Endo et al., 2014; Gravel et al., 2013; Hall et al., 2010; Doksani et al., 2013; Griffith et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2004; de Lange, 2018; Schmutz et al., 2017; Stansel et al., 2001; Van Ly et al., 2018; Pickett et al., 2009; Pickett et al., 2011; Sarek et al., 2015; Tomaska et al., 2019; Fekairi, 2009; Vannier et al., 2012; Wan et al., 2013; Deng et al., 2013; Rivera et al., 2017). These claims establish the mechanistic framework for understanding viral genome excision.

result: The study exploited the hypervariable DRR-pvT1 region to distinguish HHV-6B strains. Analysis of 102 DNA samples (39 iciHHV-6B, 63 acqHHV-6B) revealed that 93 of 102 repeat patterns were different, with 61/63 (96.8%) acqHHV-6B and 30/39 (77.0%) iciHHV-6B showing unique patterns. In eight families, 18/20 children (90%) had the same repeat pattern as one parent, with maternal transmission in six families and paternal transmission in one, demonstrating predominantly maternal transmission of acqHHV-6B.
evaluation: Claims C25-C26, C33-C42, and C50 are supported by experimental data presented in the study (Figures 1, 1-supplement 1, 1-supplement 2). The DRR-pvT1 analysis successfully distinguished between HHV-6B strains with high specificity (96.8% unique patterns in acqHHV-6B), and family transmission patterns were clearly documented. The CEPH1375 family control (C41-C42) demonstrated stability of repeat patterns across three generations, validating the approach. The methodology is sound and the conclusions are well-supported by the data.

result: The study sequenced 10 iciHHV-6A and 5 iciHHV-6B genomes, confirming that most iciHHV-6A genomes in European and North American carriers originate from three integration events at 17p, 18q, and 19q (23-105 thousand years ago), while iciHHV-6B carriers originate from more recent, numerous integration events (21-25 thousand years ago). Two new iciHHV-6B clades were identified, and potentially inactivating mutations in U14 and U79 were shown to have arisen after integration.
evaluation: Claims C43-C47 are supported by phylogenetic analysis of newly sequenced genomes combined with previously published sequences (Figure 2, Figure 2-supplement 1). The phylogenetic networks reinforce prior findings (Aswad et al., 2021; Greninger et al., 2018; Tweedy et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017) and add new information with two new iciHHV-6B clades. The HHV-6 Explorer tool was used to identify post-integration mutations, providing strong evidence that these mutations arose after integration. The methodology is rigorous and conclusions are well-supported.

result: Individuals with 9q iciHHV-6B have a characteristic (CTATGG-TTAGTG-CTATGG) motif in the central region of DRR-pvT1, and viral sequences assigned to the 17p (major) iciHHV-6B group have a characteristic (GTAGTG) repeat at the fifth position.
evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are supported by data presented in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 3. The characteristic motifs were identified through analysis of DRR-pvT1 repeat patterns in samples with known integration sites (determined by genome sequence identity, FISH, or subtelomere-iciHHV-6B junction sequences). The patterns are consistent across multiple samples within each integration group, supporting the validity of these characteristic features.

result: Low-level HHV-6B was detected in 44/52 (84.6%) saliva samples with a mean of 0.00145 copies per cell. Using STELA, an average of 0.95% (range 0-1.98%) of HHV-6B genomes showed evidence of telomeric integration (pvT1 amplification). The DR:PAC1 ratio in acqHHV-6B samples was approximately 2:2, indicating most acqHHV-6B genomes are not integrated, consistent with the majority being present as viral particles in saliva.
evaluation: Claims C51-C56, C81-C82 are supported by ddPCR and STELA data (Figure 4, Supplementary file 4). The methodology included appropriate controls (HT1080 negative control with 900 STELA reactions showing no products, C96) and validation steps (sequencing of DRL-pvT1 to confirm strain identity). The authors appropriately note that the integration frequency estimates should be interpreted cautiously due to stochastic effects from low copy numbers and reduced PCR efficiency for longer molecules. The conclusion that some acqHHV-6B genomes acquire telomeres in vivo is well-supported, though the quantification has acknowledged limitations.

result: The frequency of DRL-T2 truncations with novel telomere formation averaged 1 in 120 cells but varied significantly between cell types: lowest in blood (1 in 300) and saliva (1 in 320), intermediate in sperm (1 in 160), and highest in LCLs (1 in 70) and pluripotent cells (1 in 70). TSA treatment increased truncation frequency from 0.0162 to 0.0290 per cell, suggesting chromatin conformation influences excision. A high percentage of newly formed telomeres at DRL-T2 were lengthened, particularly in pluripotent cells and blood, consistent with telomerase activity.
evaluation: Claims C57-C65, C83-C86 are supported by STELA data from multiple cell types and individuals (Figure 5, Supplementary file 5). The methodology included appropriate controls and validation: sequencing of lengthened amplicons confirmed they contained expected flanking sequences followed by (TTAGGG) repeats exceeding DRL-T2 length (C63), telomerase activity was detected in LCLs (C64), and circular DR molecules were detected by inverse PCR (C60). Statistical analysis showed significant differences between cell types (Mann-Whitney test, p-values provided). The TSA experiment (C61-C62) included biological and technical replicates with appropriate statistical testing (Wilcoxon test). The conclusion that tissues are mosaic for different iciHHV-6B compositions is well-supported by the high truncation frequencies observed.

result: Differences between DRR-pvT1 and DRL-pvT1 within single iciHHV-6B genomes were found in 24/35 (68.6%) samples. Truncations at DRR-T1 with novel telomere formation were detected in all 10 iciHHV-6B samples with larger pvT1 size differences, with frequencies varying between samples (0.0002-0.0029 per cell).
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by data presented in Figure 6, Figure 6-supplement 1, and Supplementary file 6. The two-step STELA approach successfully distinguished between telomeres at DRR-T1 and DRL-T1 based on pvT1 size differences. The methodology was validated by sequencing to confirm DRR-pvT1 patterns. The detection of truncations at DRR-T1 in all 10 samples tested provides strong evidence for this excision mechanism, though the sample selection was biased toward those with larger pvT1 differences.

result: Three individuals carry iciHHV-6B DR-only genomes (308006, SAL018, KEN071). DR-only iciHHV-6B in SAL018 and KEN071 share the common 17p (major) subtelomere-iciHHV-6B junction found in full-length iciHHV-6B carriers (801018, d44), and DR-only 308006 shares a junction with full-length carriers 401027 and 410005. This demonstrates that DR-only status has arisen independently at least twice by germline excision of U-DR in ancestors with full-length iciHHV-6B genomes.
evaluation: Claims C69-C72, C89-C92 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 3) and subtelomere-iciHHV-6B junction sequencing (Figure 3C). The shared integration sites between full-length and DR-only carriers at two different chromosome ends provide strong evidence that DR-only status arose by germline excision. The detection of DRR-T1 truncations in sperm DNA (C68) supports the plausibility of germline excision events. The conclusion that this is a relatively common event is supported by the independent occurrence at two different sites and the measurable frequency of DRR-T1 truncations in sperm.

result: In family Rx-F3a, the mother (G3P2) is an iciHHV-6B carrier, her daughter (G4P3) has two copies of iciHHV-6B (one maternal), and her son (G4P1) has 0.00025 copies per cell of HHV-6B with the same DRR-pvT1 repeat pattern as the mother. This unique repeat pattern was not seen outside this family among 102 patterns analyzed, strongly suggesting iciHHV-6B genome excision occurred in the mother and reactivated HHV-6B was transmitted to the non-iciHHV-6B son.
evaluation: Claims C73-C80, C93 are supported by ddPCR quantification and DRR-pvT1 analysis (Figure 7, Figure 7-supplement 1). The evidence is compelling: (1) the son has a very low viral load consistent with acqHHV-6B, (2) the DRR-pvT1 pattern in the son is identical to the mother's iciHHV-6B, (3) this pattern is unique among 102 samples analyzed, and (4) the daughter inherited one copy from the mother (proven by identical pattern) and presumably one from the father. While the father was not available for testing (C74, C80), the convergence of evidence strongly supports the conclusion of viral transmission from iciHHV-6B mother to non-iciHHV-6B son. The authors appropriately use cautious language ('strongly suggest', 'probable').

result: Some copies of acqHHV-6B in saliva from healthy adults gained a telomere (indicative of integration and latency), the frequency of viral genome excision from telomeres in iciHHV-6B carriers is surprisingly high and varies between tissues, newly formed short telomeres are frequently lengthened (particularly in telomerase-expressing pluripotent cells), iciHHV-6B carriers are mosaic for different iciHHV-6B structures including circular extra-chromosomal forms with reactivation potential, and iciHHV-6B can readily transition between telomere-integrated and free virus forms.
evaluation: Claims C27-C30, C32 represent the major conclusions of the study and are supported by the collective evidence from multiple experimental approaches: STELA detection of acqHHV-6B with telomeres (C27, supported by C51-C56, C81-C82), high frequencies of DRL-T2 and DRR-T1 truncations (C28, supported by C57-C68, C83-C84), telomere lengthening particularly in pluripotent cells (C29, supported by C63-C65, C85-C86), detection of circular DR molecules (C30, supported by C60), and transmission from iciHHV-6B mother to non-iciHHV-6B son (C32, supported by C73-C80, C93). The conclusions are well-supported by converging lines of evidence from multiple experimental approaches with appropriate controls and validation.

result: The study shows transmission of an HHV-6B strain from an iciHHV-6B mother to her non-iciHHV-6B son.
evaluation: Claim C31 is supported by the detailed evidence from family Rx-F3a (C73-C80, C93, Figure 7). The convergence of evidence (unique DRR-pvT1 pattern, low viral load in son consistent with acqHHV-6B, identical pattern to mother's iciHHV-6B) strongly supports this conclusion. This represents a key finding demonstrating that iciHHV-6B can reactivate and be transmitted as acqHHV-6B.

result: The authors propose that iciHHV-6A/6B genomes are more likely to be excised and reactivated in undifferentiated or pluripotent cells, and that genome excision, viral gene expression, or full reactivation has the potential to be deleterious during early development.
evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are speculative proposals based on inference from the data (high excision frequencies in pluripotent cells, increased excision with TSA treatment). While the observations supporting these proposals are sound (C59, C61-C62, C86), the claims about developmental consequences (C88) are extrapolations that require additional experimental validation. The authors appropriately cite Miura et al., 2020 for the developmental concerns, but direct evidence for deleterious effects during early development is not provided in this study.

result: Screening of the BIOSTAT-CHF cohort identified 19 iciHHV-6A/6B-positive samples (9 iciHHV-6A, 0.36%, and 10 iciHHV-6B, 0.40%, one DR-only). Five iciHHV-6B carriers were identified among saliva donors. No STELA products were generated from HT1080 control among 900 reactions (4.5 μg DNA).
evaluation: Claims C94-C96 are supported by screening data and appropriate negative controls. The BIOSTAT-CHF screening (C94) identified iciHHV-6A/6B carriers at frequencies consistent with the expected ~1% prevalence (C9). The saliva donor screening (C95) identified carriers with various iciHHV-6B structures. The HT1080 negative control (C96) is critical for validating the specificity of the STELA approach for detecting acqHHV-6B integration, demonstrating no false-positive amplification from other telomeres or genomic regions.
